comments.author: Sidnioulz
comments.body: Attn: this will cause a shell script to be passed on to a Node runtime. It will most likely cause bugs for other users.
comments.label_reasoning: The comment warns that shell scripts will be incorrectly passed to the Node runtime, meaning the code behavior does not match its intent of executing shell scripts.

comments.author: robbchar
comments.body: Yes, definitely, that was the bug though, right? https://github.com/storybookjs/storybook/issues/32949 My thought was that the reporter has that setup intentionally so that something happens in addition to the browser running.

comments.author: Sidnioulz
comments.body:
They want it to be called, but probably not by a Node runtime. Rather, by a Shell runtime. `xdg-open` will not run in Node.

I believe the way to handle this would be to add an `Actions` type for shell and to spawn a shell interpreter. Which leads to the question: what operating systems are expected to have .sh? Should POSIX be assumed? Should the presence of `bash` be assumed?

comments.author: robbchar
comments.body:
Good questions. They weren't specific with the use-case, I was thinking the user would deal with the actual running of the script and the things within the script. I _bet_ storybook doesn't really want to be in the business of figuring out OS's/shells that kind of thing. 

If we do want to go down that route then I feel like we could decide things like what's assumed, Though actually spawning off a node script, or trying to, seems like pretty good 'best effort' for something that is not the main purpose of storybook.

comments.author: robbchar
comments.body: Agree that passing .sh to Node would be wrong; we either need a shell branch or drop .sh from this path. Since Storybook likely doesn’t want to manage cross-platform shell execution, I propose we support Node-run scripts only and remove .sh here.

comments.author: Sidnioulz
comments.body: If the goal of the issue is to support xdg-open users, who rely on FreeDesktop.org standards (including most Linux and some BSD users), then surely it's fine to restrict `.sh` execution to POSIX compliant systems e.g. Linux, BSD, Mac and WSL. We can just call bash like we call node (even though users could prefer another JS interpreter).

comments.author: robbchar
comments.body: Oh wait, so I said 'thumbs up' but I thought of something else. This is for what I would call 'xdg-open'-like users in that they don't have xdg-open but rather some script, that presumably acts in the same way. I'm still going to implement it to work POSIX systems.

comments.author: coderabbitai
comments.body:
_⚠️ Potential issue_ | _🔴 Critical_

**Test validates incorrect behavior for shell script execution.**

This test confirms that shell scripts are executed via `spawn(process.execPath, ...)`, where `process.execPath` is the Node.js binary. Node.js cannot execute shell scripts, so this test documents behavior that will fail at runtime.

Until shell scripts are properly handled with a shell interpreter (see critical issue in opener.ts lines 37-43), consider either:
1. Remove this test and only add .mjs/.cjs extensions to the implementation, which work with Node
2. Update both implementation and test to properly execute shell scripts using a shell interpreter
3. Change the test to verify .js/.mjs/.cjs files instead of .sh



Related to the critical issue raised in opener.ts at lines 37-43.

comments.author: coderabbitai
comments.body:
_⚠️ Potential issue_ | _🔴 Critical_

**Critical: Shell scripts cannot be executed by Node.js runtime.**

The code routes .sh files to `Actions.SCRIPT`, which causes `executeNodeScript` (line 166) to spawn them using `process.execPath` (the Node.js binary). Node.js cannot execute shell scripts—they require a shell interpreter like `/bin/sh` or `/bin/bash`.

This implementation will fail at runtime with syntax errors when Node attempts to parse shell scripts as JavaScript. To properly support shell scripts:

1. Add a separate action type (e.g., `Actions.SHELL_SCRIPT`) for .sh files
2. Create a new handler function that detects the appropriate shell interpreter and spawns scripts using it (e.g., `spawn('/bin/sh', [scriptPath, url], ...)` on POSIX systems)
3. Keep `.js`, `.mjs`, and `.cjs` in the current `Actions.SCRIPT` path since they are valid Node.js files

Alternatively, if determining the shell interpreter adds too much complexity, document that only Node.js scripts (.js/.mjs/.cjs) are supported via BROWSER and remove .sh from this condition.



Related to past review discussion: this confirms the concern that shell scripts will be incorrectly passed to Node runtime.

<details>
<summary>🤖 Prompt for AI Agents</summary>

```
In code/core/src/core-server/utils/open-browser/opener.ts around lines 37 to 43,
the code classifies ".sh" files as Actions.SCRIPT which causes the Node runtime
to be used to execute shell scripts and fail; change the logic to treat ".sh"
separately by adding a new action (e.g., Actions.SHELL_SCRIPT) or remove ".sh"
from this branch; if adding the action, implement a corresponding handler that
spawns the appropriate shell interpreter (detect POSIX vs Windows) and invokes
the script with the URL argument, otherwise document/support only Node scripts
and ensure only .js/.mjs/.cjs map to Actions.SCRIPT.
```

</details>

comments.author: coderabbitai
comments.body:
_⚠️ Potential issue_ | _🟠 Major_

<details>
<summary>🧩 Analysis chain</summary>

🏁 Script executed:

```shell
fd "opener.test.ts" --type f
```

Repository: storybookjs/storybook

Length of output: 186

---

🏁 Script executed:

```shell
cat -n code/core/src/core-server/utils/open-browser/opener.test.ts
```

Repository: storybookjs/storybook

Length of output: 186

---

🌐 Web query:

`Node.js process.platform property descriptor non-configurable read-only Object.defineProperty`

💡 Result:

Short answer: process.platform is a non-writable data property (so assignment won't change it) but is defined as enumerable and configurable on current Node builds — you can override it with Object.defineProperty but not by simple assignment. Example descriptor seen in practice:

Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(process, 'platform')
// -> { value: 'darwin' /*or other*/, writable: false, enumerable: true, configurable: true }. [1][2]

Notes:
- Because writable is false you cannot change it with =; use Object.defineProperty(process, 'platform', { value: 'x' }) to override in tests. [2][1]
- If a property is non-configurable, redefining it throws a TypeError; use Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor first to inspect attributes before redefining. [3]

Sources:
[1] Node.js process.platform docs.  
[2] Example / discussion showing Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(process, 'platform').  
[3] MDN: "can't redefine non-configurable property" (behavior when configurable is false).

---

🌐 Web query:

`Vitest vi.spyOn process.platform get stub Node.js testing best practices`

💡 Result:

Short answer — preferred options and best practices:

1) Best (Vitest) way — spy the getter and restore:
- Use vi.spyOn(process, 'platform', 'get') to mock the getter, then mockReturnValue / mockImplementation and restore with mockRestore() or afterEach. This keeps changes scoped and reversible.
  Example:
  const spy = vi.spyOn(process, 'platform', 'get').mockReturnValue('linux')
  // test...
  spy.mockRestore()
- Rationale: vi.spyOn supports spying/mocking getters and integrates with Vitest restore helpers. [1][3]

2) Alternative (low-level) — defineProperty override:
- Use Object.defineProperty(process, 'platform', { value: 'linux' }) in beforeEach and restore the saved descriptor in afterEach. Works when spyOn cannot reach the internal property. Keep it scoped and restore to avoid cross-test leaks. [4]

3) Another Vitest helper — stubGlobal for entire global:
- vi.stubGlobal('process', { ... }) or stub only the needed globals if you must change global object; unstub with vi.unstubAllGlobals or explicit restoration. Use sparingly — it affects all tests. [2]

4) Best practices / caveats:
- Always restore after each test (mockRestore, vi.unstubAllGlobals, or restore descriptor) to avoid flakiness. [1][3]
- Prefer dependency injection or feature-flagging (pass platform as an argument or wrapper) instead of mutating process.platform when possible — safer and simpler to test.
- Be careful: overriding process.platform can break other modules or Node internals and child processes; keep scope minimal and document the mock. [4]

References:
- Vitest vi.spyOn / mocking docs. [1][3]
- vi.stubGlobal docs. [2]
- Common Node technique using Object.defineProperty to override process.platform (practical examples / caveats). [4]

---



</details>

**Use `vi.spyOn()` with getter spy instead of `Object.defineProperty()` for safer platform mocking across environments**

`process.platform` in Node.js is read-only but configurable in current builds, so `Object.defineProperty()` technically works. However, the property's configurability can vary across Node versions and environments, making this approach brittle. Additionally, direct property mutation bypasses Vitest's spy helpers and can leak across tests if not carefully restored.

Use getter spies instead for better safety, reliability, and automatic restoration:

```ts
beforeEach(() => {
  vi.spyOn(process, 'platform', 'get').mockReturnValue('linux');
});

afterEach(() => {
  vi.restoreAllMocks();
});
```

This approach:
- Works consistently across Node versions
- Integrates with Vitest's cleanup helpers
- Automatically scopes changes and prevents test pollution
- Aligns with Storybook's spy mocking patterns

Also applies to: 18-23, 31-35, 76-80, 92-97, 108-113, 124-129

<summary>🤖 Prompt for AI Agents</summary>

```
In code/core/src/core-server/utils/open-browser/opener.test.ts around lines
14-16 (and also apply similar changes at 18-23, 31-35, 76-80, 92-97, 108-113,
124-129), tests currently mutate process.platform via Object.defineProperty
which is brittle and can leak; replace those direct property definitions with
Vitest getter spies (vi.spyOn(process, 'platform', 'get').mockReturnValue(...))
in the appropriate beforeEach blocks and add vi.restoreAllMocks() in afterEach
to ensure automatic cleanup and avoid leaking across tests.
```

</details>

comments.body:
```suggestion

```

POSIX does not mandate use of `/bin/`, but Node.js spawn should lookup commands through `$PATH`, ensuring that `sh` is found regardless of install location.
comments.label_reasoning: Using '/bin/sh' hardcodes a path that may not exist on all POSIX systems, while 'sh' via PATH lookup is the portable and correct approach — the hardcoded path deviates from correct cross-platform intent.

comments.author: coderabbitai
comments.body:
_⚠️ Potential issue_ | _🟡 Minor_

**Document TypeScript runtime requirements for .ts script execution.**

Executing `.ts` files requires Node.js v22.18.0+ with `--experimental-strip-types` flag, or v24+ for basic TypeScript (erasable syntax only). For TypeScript features like enums, `--experimental-transform-types` is required. Consider adding a version check or documenting this limitation, as the current code doesn't handle necessary runtime flags or fallbacks for earlier Node versions.
